courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
question: An analyst counts victims on a group's leak site to estimate how many organisations it attacked last month. Why is this estimate unreliable?
options: Groups like LockBit list only victims who refused to pay, and publication can lag the attack by months
Leak sites list victims only after payment
Leak sites are always fake
Leak sites only list victims outside the US
explain: CISA's LockBit advisory says leak sites show only the portion of victims who did not pay, and that publication dates can be months after the attack. Leak sites are real evidence, just incomplete and delayed.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
question: Which change would fix the fail-open pattern in the model?
options: Add another elif comparing against a third hash
Hash the empty password before comparing
Make the final else return False and require a positive match to return True
Log failed logins
explain: Fail-closed means that the only way to succeed is to pass a check; everything else, including missing input, is denied. Adding comparisons keeps the permissive default; logging detects but does not prevent.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The ransom decision: negotiation, proof of life and sanctions
question: Since 7 May 2024, why is a payment to a LockBit affiliate a much larger legal risk for a US company?
options: Cryptocurrency payments became illegal in the US
The UK ban applies to US companies
The FBI must approve every ransom payment
LockBit's leader is designated by the US Treasury, and payments reaching a designated person can violate OFAC rules on a strict liability basis
explain: Under LockBit's model the affiliate receives the ransom and sends the core its cut (lesson 1), so part of any payment reaches the designated leader. OFAC rules prohibit dealings with designated persons on a strict liability basis; cooperation with law enforcement is a mitigating factor. US law does not ban cryptocurrency or require FBI approval, and the UK announcement does not bind US firms.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A peer's RDMA WRITE targets `remote_addr = 0x15040` in the 8-page region starting at `0x10000` (4 KB pages). Which page index and byte offset does the NIC write?
options: Page 4, offset 0x40
Page 5, offset 0x400
Page 5, offset 64
Page 21, offset 64
explain: Offset = 0x15040 - 0x10000 = 0x5040 = 20544 bytes. 20544 / 4096 = 5 remainder 64. So page index 5 at byte 64 (0x40). Page 21 comes from forgetting to subtract the base.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: A 64-node cluster with 24 threads per node uses one RC QP between every pair of threads. Using FaRM's formula, how many QPs does each machine hold, and what is the likely symptom?
options: 2 x 64 x 24 = 3072; none, QPs are free
64 x 24 = 1536; the CQ overflows
24 x 24 = 576; RNR errors
2 x 64 x 24 x 24 = 73,728; throughput drops from QP-state cache misses on the NIC
explain: 2mt squared = 2 x 64 x 576 = 73,728. QP state lives in host memory with the NIC caching it; FaRM saw request rates fall as the cluster grew for exactly this reason. One QP per thread per machine (3072) or sharing among q threads cuts it.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
question: A racing game with heavy, fast cars shows remote cars stuttering. Which technique fits best before adding interpolation delay?
options: Dead reckoning from last known speed and heading, corrected by each update
Lag compensation
Server reconciliation of remote cars
Masking WebSocket frames
explain: A fast car cannot change direction instantly, so its position is predictable from speed and heading: the classic case for dead reckoning. Lag compensation is about hit tests; reconciliation applies to your own inputs.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Matrix factorization: learning user and item vectors
question: You have billions of implicit events (every user-item pair counts) and a cluster of machines. Which optimizer do Koren et al. suggest, and why?
options: SGD, because it is always faster than ALS
Neither; matrix factorization cannot use implicit data
SGD with a larger learning rate, to make up for the dense data
ALS, because each user (and each item) vector is an independent least-squares solve that parallelizes, and it avoids looping over every cell of a dense matrix
explain: Both reasons are stated in the paper: ALS parallelizes naturally, and for implicit data the training set is not sparse, so per-cell SGD loops are impractical. Hu et al. show how ALS stays linear in the number of non-zeros.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
question: Your new model beats matrix factorization on a random 80/20 holdout of watch events. Before shipping, what is the most important check?
options: Re-run with a different random seed for the same 80/20 split
Evaluate with a temporal split (train on the past, predict later events) against tuned baselines, then A/B test
Switch the metric from recall@k to RMSE
Add more epochs until offline recall stops improving
explain: A random holdout lets the model see a user's future and future popularity. A temporal split matches deployment, tuned simple baselines guard against weak comparisons (Dacrema et al.), and only an online test measures the real effect.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
question: The outer side of a join yields 10 rows after a filter. The inner table has 10000 rows and a B-tree index on the join key. Which plan is most likely cheapest?
options: Nested loop with an index scan on the inner side
Hash join, building on the 10000-row table
Merge join after sorting both sides
Nested loop with a sequential scan of the inner side
explain: Ten index lookups touch only a few pages each, while a hash join must read all 10000 inner rows once. The PostgreSQL docs show exactly this case (unique1 < 10) choosing Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan. A nested loop with a sequential inner scan would read the 10000-row table 10 times.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
question: A web app writes a profile update to the primary, then immediately reads it from a synchronous standby configured with `synchronous_commit = on`. Users sometimes see the old profile. Why?
options: The standby is asynchronous despite the setting
Synchronous replication only applies to DDL (data definition language: schema-changing) statements
The standby flushed the WAL record but had not yet replayed it when the read arrived
The primary acknowledged before flushing its own WAL
explain: `on` waits for the standby to flush the commit record to disk, not to apply it. Replay is a separate step, so a read can arrive in between. `remote_apply` closes that gap at a higher commit latency, or the app can read its own writes from the primary.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
question: Vector clocks: version X = [(Sx,3),(Sy,1)] and version Y = [(Sx,2),(Sy,2)]. What should a Dynamo-style store do on a read that finds both?
options: Return both as concurrent siblings
Keep X, since Sx's counter is larger
Keep Y, since it has the larger total
Keep whichever has the later wall-clock timestamp
explain: X is ahead on Sx (3 vs 2) but behind on Sy (1 vs 2), so neither descends from the other. They are concurrent, and the store returns both for reconciliation. Picking by one counter, a sum or a wall clock would silently drop an update.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
question: A judge's fitted length-controlled model gives your model theta = 0.4. Its raw win rate is 80 percent and its answers are much longer than the baseline's. What is its LC win rate?
options: 80 percent: length control only matters for shorter answers
50 percent: length control resets every model to even
40 percent: theta read as a probability
About 60 percent: the logistic of 0.4, the predicted win rate at equal length
explain: Setting the length difference to 0 leaves sigma(theta) = 1/(1 + e^-0.4), about 0.599. Theta is a log-odds, not a probability, and LC does not reset models to 50 percent: only a model as good as the baseline at equal length gets 50.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
question: A team evaluates a support agent on 500 single-turn prompts and finds no policy violations. In production the agent retries after API errors and sees its earlier messages. What does Pan et al. (2024) suggest?
options: The result transfers, since the weights are identical
Strengthen the system prompt and ship
Evaluate with multi-step feedback loops and injected errors, because ICRH grows with cycles of feedback that a static evaluation never runs
Switch to a larger model
explain: ICRH is a feedback-loop phenomenon: violations grew with rounds of error feedback in ToolEmu. A single-turn test runs zero cycles. The paper found larger models sometimes worse and better-specified prompts unlikely to fix it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Putting money on risk: ALE and the FAIR model
question: Laptop theft: asset value USD 1,500, exposure factor 1.0, about 4 thefts a year. A control costs USD 5,000 a year and halves the theft rate. Based on ALE alone, is it worth it?
options: Yes, it saves USD 6,000 a year
Yes, any control that halves risk is worth it
No: ALE falls from USD 6,000 to 3,000, saving USD 3,000 for USD 5,000
Cannot compute without FAIR
explain: SLE = 1,500; ALE = 1,500 x 4 = 6,000; with the control ALE = 3,000. Saving 3,000 a year for 5,000 a year loses money, unless the laptops hold data whose breach costs more, which would change the SLE.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
question: A company excludes Annex A control 7.4 (physical security monitoring) in its SoA. When is that acceptable?
options: Never; all 93 controls are mandatory
When the exclusion is justified, for example no premises in scope and the cloud provider's physical controls are covered elsewhere
Only if the CEO signs it
Only in the first year of certification
explain: Clause 6.1.3 d) requires justification for excluding Annex A controls. A justified exclusion is fine; an unjustified one is a nonconformity.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
question: The plan check passes, but an engineer later disables encryption on a bucket by hand in the AWS console. What catches it?
options: Nothing can catch it
A live-configuration check (for example an AWS Config rule) or the nightly evidence snapshot, plus Terraform drift detection
The same plan check on the next pull request, always
The SOC 2 report
explain: Plan checks see only changes made through Terraform. Manual changes need detection on the live account: config rules, scheduled snapshots, or terraform plan showing drift.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
question: An auditor finds the policy says 'all laptops use full-disk encryption' but the device report shows 7 percent unencrypted. Which response best fixes the problem?
options: Change the policy to 'most laptops'
Enforce encryption through device management so unencrypted laptops cannot reach company systems, record exceptions for the rest with expiry dates, and keep the device report as evidence
Send a reminder email
Remove the policy
explain: Make the system enforce the rule, handle real exceptions explicitly, and let the enforcement produce evidence. Rewording or reminders leave the gap open.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: In the toy model, the 16,000-token response is replaced by one of 4000 tokens. What happens to the synchronous rollout time?
options: It drops to 80 s, because every engine now finishes at 4000 tokens
It drops from 320 s to 122 s, because engine 3's 6100-token response becomes the longest
It stays at 320 s, because the batch size is unchanged
It drops to about 79 s, the mean length times 20 ms
explain: A synchronous batch ends when its longest response ends. Without the 16k response the longest is 6100 tokens on engine 3, so 6100 x 20 ms = 122 s. The mean sets throughput only if nothing waits for the tail.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: Your synchronous colocated run spends 80% of each step in rollout, and one response in each batch runs to the 32k cap. Which plan addresses the root cause with the least algorithmic risk first?
options: Fully async with staleness 16 and no importance correction
Add training GPUs
Partial rollouts or a one-step overlap with bounded staleness and decoupled importance weights, then measure accuracy against a synchronous baseline
Lower the cap to 2k tokens
explain: The root cause is waiting on the long tail. Partial rollouts or a small, bounded staleness keep GPUs busy while keeping data nearly on-policy, and the decoupled objective corrects what remains. Large unbounded staleness risks learning quality; more trainers do not touch rollout; a tight cap truncates real reasoning.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: The four golden signals, read as distributions
question: Which single measurement best distinguishes the hypothesis that catalog is itself saturated from the hypothesis that catalog's database got slow?
options: Catalog's p99 latency, which is 1000 ms either way
Catalog's error rate of 7.41 percent
The number of catalog pods firing alerts
Catalog's pool wait time against its database query time: 988 ms waiting for a connection versus 12 ms executing the query
explain: p99, error rate and alert count are identical under both hypotheses, so none of them discriminates. Splitting the latency into time spent waiting for a resource and time spent doing work does: the query still takes 12 ms, so the database is fine and the backlog is in front of the pool. Instrument the wait and the work separately, or you cannot tell these apart during an incident.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
question: Your organisation writes excellent postmortems and the same class of incident keeps recurring. Which measurement would tell you where the process is leaking?
options: Mean time to resolution for the recurring class
Number of postmortems written per quarter
The fraction of action items with an owner, a bug and a priority that were completed, broken down by type
Number of alerts fired per incident
explain: Writing the document is not the mechanism that reduces recurrence; completing the typed, owned, tracked items is. Counting postmortems measures effort, and MTTR measures response rather than prevention. If completion is low, the leak is in prioritisation; if completion is high and recurrence continues, the items are not naming the right conditions.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: You are writing a Rust driver and need a C function from a subsystem that has no Rust abstraction yet. What does kernel policy expect?
options: Call it through `bindings::` inside an `unsafe` block in the driver, with a SAFETY comment
Add (or extend) a safe abstraction for it in the subsystem's Rust code, and use that from the driver
Rewrite the C function in Rust inside the driver so no FFI is needed
Use `extern "C"` to declare the function by hand in the driver
explain: The general-information doc says leaf modules such as drivers should not use the C bindings directly; subsystems provide as-safe-as-possible abstractions. Declaring the symbol yourself is the same forbidden shortcut with less checking. Duplicating the C logic would create a second implementation to maintain.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
question: A callback receives `t: &Task`. You want a work item to log that task's pid a few seconds later. What do you store in the work item?
options: `ARef::from(t)`: it takes a reference with get_task_struct and drops it with put_task_struct when the work item is dropped
`t` itself, as a `&'static Task` obtained with `core::mem::transmute`
`Arc::new(t)`, which shares the task between the callback and the work item
A bitwise copy of the C `task_struct`
explain: Only the ARef owns an increment of the task's real count. The transmuted reference compiles but nothing keeps the task alive: a use-after-free waiting to happen. `Arc::new(t)` would allocate a new object holding a borrowed `&Task` whose lifetime still ends with the callback, so it does not extend anything. Copying a task_struct copies pointers it does not own.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: Code under review creates `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` once to read and validate a header, then creates a second `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` to read the whole request and use it. What is the problem?
options: It is a double fetch: user memory can change between the two readers, so the validated header is not the one being used
Nothing: `copy_from_user` re-validates the data on every call
It cannot compile, because a `UserSlice` can only be created once per address
The second reader starts where the first one stopped, so it misses the header
explain: Each reader consumes its own UserSlice and advances independently, so the second one starts at the beginning again. `copy_from_user` checks the *address range*, not the contents. The uaccess.rs docs show exactly this pattern labelled as a TOCTOU bug and advise one UserSlice per user memory block.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
question: Your enqueue inserts a task into custom DSQ 3 while CPU 5 is idle. Nothing kicks CPU 5, and the other CPUs never read DSQ 3 in their dispatch. What can happen?
options: CPU 5 polls custom DSQs and notices within one tick
The kernel moves custom DSQ tasks to the global DSQ after one slice
The task waits while CPU 5 stays idle, until some CPU happens to dispatch from DSQ 3 or the watchdog fires
The verifier rejects enqueue callbacks that do not kick a CPU
explain: An idle CPU runs the scheduling path only when it is woken: by select_cpu choosing it, by a kick, or by new work in its local DSQ. Custom DSQs are only read by dispatch callbacks, so an unread queue plus no kick leaves the task stranded.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
question: After loading your scheduler, SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events climbs steadily. What does it point to?
options: The scheduler keeps entering bypass mode
Tasks are being inserted without a slice
Your select_cpu returns CPUs the tasks cannot use, and the core silently picks another one
The watchdog is about to declare a stall
explain: The kernel docs define it as ops.select_cpu() returning a CPU unusable by the task, after which the core picks a fallback. Look for a missing check against p->cpus_ptr, the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Revocation at scale: CircleCI and rotating every secret at once
question: A breach report says secrets were stolen on 22 December, and you finish rotating on 9 January. Which window do you search your own logs for misuse of those secrets?
options: Only 4 January, the disclosure date
From the earliest possible compromise (16 December here) until your rotation finished on 9 January
From 22 December onward
Only after 9 January
explain: Investigate the whole period a stolen copy could have worked: from the earliest date the vendor could not rule out until your rotation completed. CircleCI's own advice was 16 December through the date you rotated.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
question: Following Google's DEK guidance, how often should you rotate a DEK?
options: Every 90 days
Whenever the KEK rotates
Never in place: generate a new DEK every time you write the data, so each DEK protects one write
Only after a breach
explain: A fresh DEK per write means there is no long-lived DEK to rotate. KEK rotation does not touch DEKs at all unless you re-wrap them, and re-wrapping changes the wrapping, not the DEK itself.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
question: In the overlap timeline, when is it safe to remove k1 from the verifiers' key set?
options: As soon as k2 is published
As soon as signing switches to k2
Once the last token signed with k1 has expired
Never; old keys must be kept forever
explain: Tokens signed by k1 keep arriving until they expire. Removing k1 earlier rejects valid tokens (an outage); keeping it forever means a stolen k1 works forever, which is the Storm-0558 failure.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
question: A service loads job descriptions from a shared message queue with `pickle.loads(msg.body)`. The queue is internal. What is the best review comment?
options: Fine: internal queues are trusted by definition
Anyone who can publish to the queue gets code execution in the worker; switch to JSON with a schema
Wrap the call in try/except so malformed messages do not crash the worker
Check isinstance(result, Job) after loading
explain: pickle runs code while loading, so whoever can write to the queue controls the worker. try/except and isinstance checks happen after the code already ran. Internal is not the same as trusted: a compromise of any producer would spread.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
question: You are reviewing a 2013-style patch that adds a new lookup type to a logging library. Which review comment best addresses the risk?
options: Add unit tests that the lookup returns the right value for a valid name
Lookups are evaluated on logged data, so this lets any logged string trigger a network fetch and code load; make it opt-in and never apply lookups to message data
Rename the plugin to make its purpose clearer
Document the new syntax in the README
explain: The danger is not that the lookup works incorrectly but that it works on attacker-controlled data. Tests of the happy path, naming and documentation do not address that. The CSRB said a focused security review of exactly this addition could have found the flaw.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
question: Why did Cloudflare's report say `>=` would have prevented Cloudbleed even though the grammar bug would still exist?
options: Because >= is faster than ==
Because a pointer that jumps past the end still satisfies p >= pe, so the parser stops instead of reading on
Because >= prevents the pointer from moving
Because Ragel only supports >=
explain: An equality check only fires if the pointer lands exactly on the end. If it skips over, == is never true. An ordering check is true for every position at or past the end, so it fails safe even when another bug moves the pointer too far.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
question: Which FFI call is correct for passing a Rust string to a C function that expects a NUL-terminated string?
options: `f(name.as_ptr() as *const c_char)` with `name: &str`
`let c = CString::new(name)?; unsafe { f(c.as_ptr()) }`
`unsafe { f(CString::new(name).unwrap().into_raw()) }` and never free it
`unsafe { f(name.to_string().as_ptr() as *const c_char) }`
explain: A &str or String has no terminating NUL, so C would read past its end. into_raw without a matching from_raw leaks memory, and unwrap panics on interior NULs. Binding the CString to a variable keeps it alive for the call and guarantees exactly one terminator.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
question: An employee connects to the office through a VPN and then opens an old telnet session to a router inside the office. Who can read the telnet password?
options: Nobody, because the VPN encrypts the whole session end to end
Only the VPN provider, which can see inside the tunnel
Anyone who can capture traffic on the office network between the VPN gateway and the router
Nobody, because telnet hashes passwords before sending them
explain: The VPN protects only the stretch from the laptop to the gateway. After the gateway the telnet packets travel in the clear across the office network. SSH would protect the session all the way to the router. Telnet sends the password as typed; it does not hash it.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
question: Which ESP setting is forbidden outright by RFC 4303?
options: AES-GCM with a 16-byte ICV
NULL encryption with HMAC-SHA-256 integrity
Both encryption and integrity set to NULL
Tunnel mode between two hosts
explain: RFC 4303 allows NULL encryption (integrity only) and, as a MAY, confidentiality-only ESP, but encryption and integrity "MUST NOT both be NULL". Tunnel mode between hosts is unusual but legal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795): deleting SSH messages by shifting a counter
question: Why is a connection using aes256-gcm@openssh.com not affected by Terrapin?
options: AES-256 has a longer key than ChaCha20
GCM derives its nonce from a separate invocation counter, not from the shifted sequence number
GCM encrypts the IGNORE message so the attacker cannot inject it
GCM connections do not send EXT_INFO
explain: The attacker shifts the implicit sequence number. ChaCha20-Poly1305 and EtM MACs use it in their integrity check, so the shift is invisible. GCM's nonce starts from a key-derived value and counts invocations independently, so it does not line up after the shift.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
question: An attacker on the path between a client and its NTS server cannot break the cryptography. What can they still do to the client's clock?
options: Nothing, NTS makes time synchronisation fully secure
Replace the time in the reply with any value
Replay an old reply to set the clock back by days
Delay packets asymmetrically, shifting the computed offset by up to half the round-trip delay
explain: Delays leave packets authentic, so NTS cannot detect them; the offset error is bounded by half the round trip (MAXDIST/2 at most). Rewriting the time or replaying old replies fails NTS's authentication and request-response matching.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
question: A team adds a GraphQL endpoint that queries the database directly, while the REST routes all pass through the authorization middleware. Which reference monitor requirement does the new endpoint break?
options: Always invoked
Tamper proof
Small enough to analyse
Open design
explain: The middleware is a reference monitor, and the new endpoint reaches the objects without calling it. Tamper proofing is about attackers modifying the checker; size is about whether it can be reviewed; open design is a separate Saltzer and Schroeder principle.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
question: A hospital wants to ensure that prescription records change only through the pharmacy system's dispensing workflow, with a pharmacist approving what a doctor writes. Which model fits best?
options: Bell-LaPadula
Biba strict integrity
Brewer-Nash
Clark-Wilson
explain: The concern is how data changes: through certified programs (the dispensing workflow) with separation of duty (doctor writes, pharmacist approves). That is Clark-Wilson. Bell-LaPadula is about disclosure, Biba about trust levels, Brewer-Nash about conflicts of interest.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
question: During a session the policy engine learns that the device is infected and revokes access. Which component carries out that decision?
options: The policy engine itself, by blocking packets
The resource, by logging the user out
The policy administrator, by signalling the PEP to terminate the session
The SIEM, by alerting an analyst
explain: The PE decides and logs; the PA executes, including revoking an earlier approval by telling the PEP to shut the connection. The PEP is what actually terminates the traffic. A SIEM alert alone does not close anything.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
question: Why does SP 800-215 put a unique application identity first among microsegmentation prerequisites?
options: Because IP addresses change and are hidden by NAT, proxies, load balancers and moving VMs, so policy written on addresses cannot say which workload is talking
Because identities are cheaper to store than addresses
Because firewalls cannot read IP headers
Because SPIFFE is required by law
explain: Policy should say which workload may call which, and only a verifiable workload identity (such as a SPIFFE ID in a short-lived certificate) survives the address changes of modern infrastructure.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
question: Enriching one alert takes about 40 seconds of API calls. Which component should do that work?
options: The receiver, before it answers the SIEM
A worker that takes the alert from the queue
The SIEM, before it sends the alert
The chat bot, when the analyst opens the case
explain: The receiver must answer fast (GitHub, for example, gives up after 10 seconds and counts the delivery as failed), so slow work belongs in workers behind the queue. Making the SIEM or chat bot do it couples your pipeline to tools you do not control.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
question: Why add jitter rather than using exponential backoff alone?
options: Jitter makes each retry faster
Without jitter the API will not accept the retry
Jitter replaces the need to honour Retry-After
Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together at every step, recreating the overload
explain: Exponential backoff with identical timing keeps failed clients in lock step. Randomising the wait spreads them out. Retry-After, when present, still sets the minimum wait.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
question: Which change prevents the attacker from closing A-2291 even if the model is fully persuaded?
options: A stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions in alerts
Blocking the phrase ignore previous instructions
Wrapping each field in its own XML tag
Removing the model's ability to close or downgrade alerts, with deterministic rules making those decisions
explain: Only removing the authority holds when the model is persuaded. Prompts and tags lower the odds (and the attacker can write the closing tag); phrase blocklists are rephrased around.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
question: A web shop's product prices are changed by an intruder so that a laptop sells for USD 1. Customers can still browse and buy, and no customer data was read. Which property was violated?
options: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Non-repudiation
explain: The data was improperly modified, which is an integrity failure. Nothing secret was read (confidentiality held) and the shop stayed up (availability held). Non-repudiation is about proving who created data, which is not the issue here.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
question: Why does the security world need CVE IDs at all?
options: They give every publicly known vulnerability one shared name that scanners, advisories and people can refer to
They encrypt vulnerability details so attackers cannot read them
They rate how dangerous a bug is
They prove the vendor has fixed the bug
explain: A CVE ID is an identifier, nothing more. Severity is CVSS's job, exploitation status is KEV's, and fix status comes from the vendor advisory. One name lets a scanner report, a vendor bulletin and a news story be matched up.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
question: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
options: A tactic is the attacker's goal at that step; a technique is a specific way of achieving it
Tactics are for Windows, techniques for Linux
Tactics are legal, techniques are illegal
There is no difference; they are synonyms
explain: MITRE describes tactics as the why (for example Credential Access) and techniques as the how (for example T1552.001 Credentials In Files). One tactic has many techniques.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing is a security control: Equifax's patch email
question: Under Equifax's 2016 patch policy, why was a 430-person email a weak control even though its content was correct?
options: The email was sent too late to matter
Nobody was officially designated as owner, so no recipient was clearly obliged to act, and nothing checked for a reply
US-CERT alerts are not trustworthy enough to act on
Emails cannot contain patch instructions
explain: The alert went out two days after disclosure, well before the May intrusion. The failure was ownership and follow-up: roles existed on paper without designees, and the report found no redundancy to confirm the right person had acted.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Whole reports: pentest and audit, read by different people
question: What does the Equifax 2015 audit case show about audit writing?
options: Audits should not include dates
Clear findings with management actions and dates are not enough on their own: something must track them and escalate missed dates
Audits are only for compliance and have no security value
The audit missed the patching problem
explain: The audit named the patching and inventory problems with actions and dates. Many were not done by the 2017 breach. The weak link was follow-through, which a report must plan for.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558, a corrected blog and the CSRB report
question: What structural choice in the CSRB report helps a sceptical reader most?
options: Using no numbers
Separating a facts section from the findings and recommendations, and numbering both reasons and recommendations
Putting the recommendations before the facts
Avoiding any footnotes
explain: Separating evidence from judgement lets readers test the conclusions; numbering lets later readers track which recommendations were adopted.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing for disclosure: vendor reports, advisories and Project Zero
question: Under Project Zero's Full 90 policy, a vendor patches on day 47. When are the details published?
options: Day 47
Day 90
Day 77, after 30 days of patch uptake
Never, because it is fixed
explain: Full X discloses X days after the report regardless of when the fix lands; the policy page's own example is a day-47 patch disclosed on day 90. Earlier only if the vendor asks, or if the bug is exploited in the wild or already public.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Build a STaR loop: sample, filter, fine-tune, repeat
question: Your rationalized rationales reach the hinted answer, but an audit shows 9 in 10 state a wrong intermediate product. What is the most direct fix?
options: Drop rationalization, or keep a hinted rationale only if its intermediate numbers also check out
Raise the sampling temperature for hinted attempts
Keep more hinted rationales per question
Fine-tune from the previous checkpoint instead of the base model
explain: The final-answer filter cannot see the flaw because the hint guarantees the answer. Either remove that path or strengthen the filter for it, for example by recomputing the product. STaR's own paper found that sampling at higher temperature raised the rate of right answers from wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
question: A team wants a model to improve its customer-support replies, has thousands of real customer questions, and has no answer key or human preference labels. Which loop fits, and what is the main risk to monitor?
options: ReST-EM with a binary correctness reward; the risk is overfitting a small problem set
AlphaZero-style tree search; the risk is lack of exploration noise
Absolute Zero; the risk is nondeterministic programs
Self-Rewarding with the model as judge; the risk is the policy exploiting the judge, for example by growing longer replies
explain: Without checkable answers, the options are a judge or a human target. Self-Rewarding needs only prompts and a seed of judging examples. Its documented risk is that the judge's biases get amplified: the paper itself saw average response length grow about 2.3x over two iterations and flagged reward hacking.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
question: Two tenants (customer organizations) of your SaaS (software as a service) product use different system prompts that define different product names. Both ask "How do I export my data?". Which design prevents one tenant from receiving the other's answer?
options: Lower the similarity threshold
Include the tenant id and template version as exact-match filters in the cache lookup
Normalize prompts to lowercase
Use a larger embedding model
explain: The user text is identical, so no threshold or embedding model can tell the two apart. The difference lives in inputs the embedding never sees, so it must be part of the cache scope.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: SSRF: making the server send your request
question: Which input is the root cause in every SSRF?
options: A user-supplied value that decides the destination (scheme, host or port) of a request the server sends
Any HTTP request that contains a URL in its body
A missing CSRF token
An outdated TLS version
explain: SSRF exists when user input controls where the server connects. A URL in a request body is harmless if the server never fetches it, and CSRF tokens protect browsers, not server-side fetches.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
question: An image service accepts PNG and JPEG uploads and also, through its imaging library, SVG. Why does that matter for XXE?
options: SVG files are always larger
SVG is XML, so the library may run an XML parser with entity support on user-supplied files
SVG cannot contain text
Browsers block SVG
explain: SVG is an XML format. If the imaging library accepts it, user uploads reach an XML parser, which is hidden XXE attack surface even though the API never mentions XML. Restrict accepted formats and harden the parser.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
question: Equifax had the Struts patch for 67 days before the attackers broke in. According to the House report, which failure also let the attack run for 76 days unseen?
options: No firewall at all
Equifax used Log4j
The attackers used IMDSv1
An expired certificate left the device that inspected ACIS traffic inactive for 19 months
explain: The device that monitored ACIS traffic was inactive while its certificate was expired. When it was renewed on 29 July 2017, suspicious traffic was spotted immediately. Monitoring that silently stops working is a classic failure.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map
question: CloudTrail shows the EC2 role of your image-resizing service listing S3 buckets from an IP address outside AWS. What does this most likely mean?
options: Normal behaviour for resizing images
CloudTrail is misconfigured
The bucket is public
The instance's temporary credentials were stolen, for example via SSRF to the metadata service, and are being used elsewhere
explain: Instance role credentials should only be used from the instance. Use from an external IP is what GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding flags. Revoke the role's sessions, find the SSRF, and check what was read.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
question: You serve a DeepSeek MLA model on 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism 8 and see far fewer concurrent requests than the KV memory should allow. What explains it, and what helps?
options: The radix tree uses too much CPU memory; disable it
MLA's single latent KV is replicated on every TP rank; enabling DP attention keeps each request's KV on one GPU
The chunked prefill size is too large; set it to 512
Expert parallelism duplicates the KV cache; lower `--ep-size`
explain: TP shards attention by heads, and MLA has no per-head KV to shard, so every rank stores the full cache. DP attention (`--attn-dp-size`) partitions requests instead, cutting duplication.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: After contraction, an important motorway is closed and its weight becomes very large. What happens to a plain CH built for the old weights?
options: Queries remain correct, since shortcuts are recomputed during each query
Shortcuts that include the motorway now carry stale weights, so the contraction (at least the weights) must be redone
Only the node order must change; shortcut weights update themselves
Nothing changes, because CH queries ignore original arc weights
explain: Shortcut weights are sums of original arc weights fixed at preprocessing time. The survey notes CH can keep its node order and rerun contraction for a new metric, but some recomputation is unavoidable. Handling frequent weight changes cheaply is what customizable methods target (next lesson).

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
question: How many butterflies does a radix-2 FFT of N = 8 samples perform?
explain: There are log2 8 = 3 stages and each stage has N/2 = 4 butterflies, so 12 in total. 64 is the number of multiply-adds in the direct DFT (N squared), and 24 is N log2 N, which counts outputs over all stages (8 per stage), two per butterfly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Your Neon float sum with one accumulator runs exactly 4x faster than scalar, never more, even on data in L1. What is the most likely next step?
options: Use 4 to 8 independent accumulators and combine them at the end
Switch to 512-bit vectors
Align the array to 64 bytes
Add -O3
explain: Both the scalar and the 1-accumulator loops are bound by add latency: one add per chain per latency period. Independent accumulators overlap the chain; on the measured M5 Pro that took 4.5x to 15.5x.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: A loop over an array of 64-byte structs reads one float field per struct. AVX2 intrinsics give almost no speedup. What is the most effective first change?
options: Use AVX-512 instead
Store that field in its own contiguous array (struct-of-arrays) so one load brings 8 useful floats
Add more accumulators
Use target_clones
explain: With array-of-structs, each useful float sits 64 bytes from the next, so a vector needs a gather or 8 separate loads and wastes most of each cache line. A separate float array gives contiguous vector loads and 16 floats per cache line.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A game allocates thousands of temporary objects while building each frame, and none of them is needed after the frame is drawn. Which allocator fits best?
options: A buddy allocator, so the temporary objects can merge back into big blocks
A slab cache per object type, so each object can be freed individually
The general-purpose malloc, because the objects have different sizes
A per-frame bump arena that is reset after the frame is drawn
explain: All objects share one lifetime that ends at a known point, which is exactly the phase-oriented pattern bump allocation is built for: each allocation is a pointer add and freeing the whole frame is one reset.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
question: Why does NIST advise against first-come, first-served handling?
options: Because older alerts are usually false positives
Because analysts work faster on new alerts
Because resources are limited and the order of work should follow risk: asset criticality, impact, how far the attack has progressed
Because SIEMs sort alerts randomly
explain: Ordering by arrival time lets the noisiest source decide what gets looked at. NIST lists risk evaluation factors such as asset criticality, functional and data impact, stage of observed activity and recoverability as the basis for triage and prioritisation.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
question: Why did the SolarWinds discovery start from a *routine* alert?
options: Because high-severity alerts were switched off
Because a careful analyst checked an MFA enrollment alert against what they knew about the user (location, existing devices, simultaneous sessions) and found contradictions
Because the backdoor itself raised the alert
Because the employee reported the phone
explain: Per Wired and NPR, the alert only said a new phone was enrolled. The analyst noticed it had no phone number, signed in from a state the employee did not live in, and was active at the same time as the employee's real phone, then called the employee. Context, not severity, made it matter.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
question: A firewall logs in local time without an offset (the appliance is set to UTC-05:00), and your EDR logs in UTC. A firewall line says 04:10 and an EDR line says 09:05. In UTC, which happened first?
options: The firewall event, at 04:10 UTC
They happened at the same moment
The EDR event: the firewall's 04:10 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR's 09:05
It cannot be determined from timestamps
explain: Local 04:10 at UTC-05:00 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR event. Ordering raw strings from mixed zones would have put the firewall event five hours earlier.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
question: Your SOC's MTTA improved from 20 to 6 minutes after a new rule let analysts bulk-close alerts from noisy rules. What should you check before celebrating?
options: Nothing; faster is better
Whether true positives are still being found and how fast they were acknowledged, and whether bulk closures carry reasons that quality review can check
Whether the analysts are working longer hours
Whether the SIEM clock is correct
explain: Speed can improve by doing less looking. The metric that matters is how quickly real attacks were caught, and whether closures are still evidence-based. That is the gaming risk the SOUPS study describes.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
question: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, which policy is allowed for a password used as a single factor?
options: Minimum 15 characters, checked against a blocklist, no composition rules
Minimum 8 characters, must contain a digit and a symbol
Must be changed every 90 days
Must have a hint so users can recover it
explain: Single-factor passwords need at least 15 characters. Composition rules, periodic changes and hints are all prohibited by SHALL NOT statements in the guideline.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: The help desk as an attack surface: MGM, Okta's warning and Clorox
question: A help desk procedure requires 'manager name and username' before a reset. What is its main weakness?
options: It takes too long
It requires a manager to be online
Both facts are often discoverable from public profiles, org charts or earlier calls, so they do not prove identity
Usernames are secret by design
explain: Mandiant's hardening guide warns against relying on publicly available personal data because the group 'often possesses this information'. Proof must be something the attacker cannot research or buy.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: What a lock really does: pin tumblers, master keys and key control
question: Why does Blaze's finding matter more for an office tower with tenants than for a single-family house?
options: Tower locks are cheaper
Houses have no locks
Many unrelated people hold change keys in the same master system, so one of them could amplify their access to all doors
Towers have more windows
explain: The attack starts from a legitimate change key and its lock. A large master-keyed system hands that starting point to many people, any of whom could derive the master.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: An employee admits they approved an MFA prompt they did not start, two hours ago. What should the first response be?
options: Schedule them for mandatory retraining before anything else
Wait to see whether anything bad happens
Reset only their password
Thank them, revoke their sessions, re-secure their factors and check what the session did
explain: The stolen session, not the password, is the attacker's access, so sessions must be revoked and factors checked. Thanking them keeps reporting alive; retraining first signals blame.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
The learning rate is too high; lower it
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Why fit a model like the spherical one instead of plugging the four empirical bin values directly into kriging?
options: The empirical values are in the wrong units
Kriging needs semivariance at arbitrary distances, and the model must be a valid one so that every predicted variance is non-negative
Spherical models always fit better than the empirical values
Fitting removes the need to choose a nugget
explain: Kriging asks for $\gamma$ at every sensor-to-sensor and sensor-to-target distance, not just the bin centers, and arbitrary numbers can produce negative variances. Valid model families avoid that.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
question: A round with gamma = 5 finds the first mismatch at guess 4 (1-based). How many tokens does it append?
explain: Guesses 1 to 3 are accepted and the target's own token replaces guess 4, giving 4 tokens. Guess 5 and the bonus slot are discarded because they were computed after a rejected token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: Your new model lowers WER on your test set from 9% to 6%, but you also switched to a normalizer that expands numbers and removes filler words. What should you conclude?
options: The model is 33% better
Nothing yet: rescore the old model with the new normalizer and compare
The old normalizer was wrong, so only the new number counts
WER is meaningless and should be replaced by human judgment
explain: Two things changed at once. The Whisper paper reports normalization alone moving WER by up to 50% on some datasets. Score both models with the same normalizer before attributing the gain to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: For virtual address 0x00007f3a12345678 mapped with a 2 MiB huge page, which bits form the offset within the page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 20 to 0
Bits 29 to 0
Bits 47 to 21
explain: A 2 MiB page is $2^{21}$ bytes, so the offset is the low 21 bits (here 0x145678). The PMD entry maps the page directly, so bits 20 to 12, which would normally index a PTE table, become part of the offset.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
question: With $T_M$ = 100 ns and $T_D$ = 10 ms, roughly what average access time does a 1 percent page-fault rate give?
options: About 100 microseconds, 1,000 times slower than RAM
About 1 microsecond
About 10 milliseconds
About 200 nanoseconds
explain: AMAT = 100 ns + 0.01 x 10 ms = 100 ns + 100 microseconds, about 100.1 microseconds, roughly 1,000 times the 100 ns memory cost. Ten times the miss rate of OSTEP's 0.1 percent example gives ten times the slowdown.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: A team builds a sycophancy vector from 500 A/B pairs, picks the layer and coefficient that maximize the score on those same 500 pairs, and reports a large effect. What is the main flaw?
options: They should have used fewer pairs
Sycophancy cannot be represented linearly
They should have reported MMLU instead of the behavior score
The vector, the hyperparameters and the reported score all come from the same data, so the effect is likely overstated; it needs held-out validation and test splits
explain: Choosing layer and c on the evaluation data overfits them to it. CAA scores on 50 held-out questions, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation, and Arditi et al. keep train, validation and evaluation sets pairwise disjoint. Capability checks are needed too, but they do not fix the leak.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses
question: What is the main cost BiPO and LoReFT pay compared with a difference-of-means vector?
options: They change all the model's weights
They cannot be applied at inference time
They need labelled or preference data and gradient-based training through the frozen model
They only work on models under 1 billion parameters
explain: Both keep the model's weights frozen and train only the intervention (a vector for BiPO, R, W and b for LoReFT), which requires backpropagation and suitable data. Difference of means needs only forward passes on contrast pairs.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Your sink appends one row per window firing. With allowed lateness 5 s, window [0,10) fires at count 4 and later at count 5. A dashboard sums all rows per window. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: The window is counted as 4 + 5 = 9 readings; write with an upsert keyed by (sensor, window) since firings are accumulating
Nothing; the second firing contains only the late reading
Late firings are never sent to sinks
The fix is to set allowed lateness higher
explain: In accumulating mode each firing is the full refined result, so appending both rows double counts. Overwrite by window key, or use discarding mode and have the consumer add deltas, or emit retractions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: Which statement about beam search with beam size B = 1 is correct?
options: It is the same as greedy decoding: only the single best partial output is kept each step
It explores every possible sentence, so it always finds the most probable one
It needs teacher forcing at inference
It is the paper's setting for the base model
explain: Keeping one hypothesis and extending it by its most probable token is exactly greedy decoding. No practical beam search explores every sentence; the paper used B = 4. Teacher forcing applies only to training.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Your index holds tweets whose lengths all fall between 25 and 35 tokens, and nothing else. You move b from 0.75 to 0.3. What do you expect?
options: Large ranking changes, because tweets vary in length
All scores become zero
Scores become probabilities
Small changes, because lengths are all close to avgdl so B stays near 1 either way
explain: B = (1 - b) + b x |d|/avgdl. When every |d|/avgdl is near 1, B is near 1 for any b, so b has little effect. b matters most when lengths vary a lot.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: The training loop end to end: data, evals, overfitting, checkpoints
question: Why does nanoGPT store OpenWebText as uint16 and not int64 like the tensors it trains on?
options: Every GPT-2 token id is at most 50,256, which fits in 16 bits, so the 9-billion-token file is 4 times smaller; get_batch converts each slice to int64
uint16 makes the tokenizer faster
PyTorch embeddings require 16-bit indices
Negative ids mark document boundaries
explain: Two bytes per token gives the 17 GB train.bin; int64 would be 72 GB. The conversion to int64 happens only for the few slices that get_batch reads. End-of-text is the ordinary id 50256, not a negative number.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: Someone computes $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2 + 1)$ at $x = 1$ and gets $1/2$. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; 1/2 is correct
They used 1/u with u = 2 but forgot to multiply by du/dx = 2x = 2; the answer is 1
They should have used 1/x, giving 1
The log has no derivative at 1
explain: Outer: $d\ln(u)/du = 1/u = 1/2$ at $u = 2$. Inner: $du/dx = 2x = 2$. The chain rule multiplies them: $1/2 \times 2 = 1$. Forgetting the inner factor is the most common chain-rule error.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Two losses are $x^2 + 3y^2$ and $x^2 + 30y^2$. Compared with the first, what happens to the largest stable learning rate for plain gradient descent on the second?
options: It stays 1/3 because the x term is unchanged
It increases, because the bowl is steeper so it is easier to find the bottom
It drops to 1/30, because the steepest direction now has a = 30
It is unlimited, because the minimum is still at the origin
explain: Using the factor $1 - 2a\eta$, the $30y^2$ term needs $\eta < 1/30$. The steepest direction caps the step size for all parameters, so the shallow $x$ direction now crawls. This mismatch is called poor conditioning.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: `grep ERROR huge.log | head -n 5` returns almost instantly even though huge.log is 50 GB. Why?
options: grep detects the head command and reads only 5 lines
head reads the file directly and grep is skipped
The kernel caches the whole file before grep starts
Once head exits after 5 lines, grep's next write raises SIGPIPE and grep dies
explain: Both run concurrently. After head has its five lines it exits, closing the read end. grep's next write to the pipe triggers SIGPIPE, ending it long before it reaches the end of the file.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
question: Your public key is in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, yet ssh falls back to asking for a password. On the server, `ls -ld ~/.ssh` shows `drwxrwxrwx`. What is the likely cause?
options: sshd will not use authorized_keys while ~/.ssh is writable by other users
The key type is wrong for this server
known_hosts on your laptop is missing
The private key must also be copied to the server
explain: Anyone who can write to `~/.ssh` could add their own key, so sshd refuses to trust authorized_keys there (its StrictModes check). `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` fix it. The private key must never be copied to the server.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
question: You change the PyTorch script to `torch.optim.Adam([v.weight, u.weight])` and keep `sparse=True`. What happens?
options: Training runs normally but uses more memory
Adam silently ignores the embedding rows
The first `opt.step()` raises an error, because Adam does not accept sparse gradients
Adam converts the gradients to dense and trains the same model
explain: PyTorch raises `RuntimeError: Adam does not support sparse gradients, please consider SparseAdam instead`. Either keep `sparse=True` with SparseAdam (or SGD), or drop `sparse=True` and use dense Adam, which then updates moment estimates for every row on every step.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias
question: Your fastText model gives the unseen word *unhappiness* a vector close to *happiness* and *sadness*. Which part of the model made that possible?
options: The context vectors of the words around *unhappiness* at query time
A shared unknown-word row
The n-gram vectors it shares with seen words, such as *hap*, *ness* and *ness>*, summed into a vector
The full softmax over the vocabulary
explain: An unseen word has no word vector, but its character n-grams were trained inside other words. fastText sums their vectors. At query time there is no context and no training, and an unknown row would give every unseen word the same vector.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: Which statement about running `./hello` is correct?
options: The shell reads hello's machine code and executes it itself
The CPU loads the ELF file from disk one instruction at a time as it runs
The kernel, via execve, replaces the current process image with hello and starts it at its entry point
The linker runs again every time you start the program
explain: execve(2): the program currently run by the calling process is replaced with a new one, with a newly initialized stack, heap and data segments. The CPU never reads from the disk file directly; pages of the file are mapped into memory and loaded when touched.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: A colleague's loop `for j: for i: total += m[i][j]` over a large C 2D array of longs is slow. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Swap the loops so the inner loop walks j along a row
Use a faster add instruction
Make total a global variable
Add more threads before changing anything
explain: In C, m[i][j] and m[i][j+1] are adjacent, so walking j in the inner loop uses all 8 longs of every 64-byte line it fetches. The current inner loop strides a full row per access, fetching a new line every time.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
question: A labeler ranks K = 6 responses. How many pairwise comparisons does that give, and how many gradient terms does each single response appear in?
options: 6 pairs; each response appears in 1
30 pairs; each response appears in 10
36 pairs; each response appears in 6
15 pairs; each response appears in 5
explain: C(6,2) = 15 pairs, and each response is compared with the other K - 1 = 5. That correlation is why InstructGPT batches all pairs from one prompt together instead of shuffling them.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: In the toy, which beta gives the best true quality among the ones shown, and why is the smallest beta not best?
options: beta = 1, because past it the policy shifts mass to the response the reward model overrates
beta = 0.1, because it has the highest reward model score
beta = 100, because any change from SFT hurts
All are equal, because the reward model is unbiased on average
explain: True quality is 0.27 at beta = 1 versus 0.24 at 0.5 and -0.38 at 0.1. Small beta lets the policy concentrate on Flattery, which the reward model overrates. Some optimization helps: beta = 100 leaves quality at 0.10.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. -O2 (optimization level 2) cannot help: the compiler can only inline a body it can see, and main.c never sees area.c. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
question: `unsigned char a = 250, b = 10; int s = a + b;` What is s?
options: Undefined behavior, because the sum overflows unsigned char
explain: Integer promotion converts a and b to int before adding, so the sum is computed as int and 260 fits. It would become 4 only if stored back into an unsigned char (260 modulo 256).

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
options: It tests errno instead of f: errno may be nonzero even though fopen succeeded
Nothing; errno is 0 whenever fopen succeeds
perror needs errno passed as an argument
fopen never sets errno, so the check never fires
explain: errno is meaningful only after a call reports failure, and a successful call is allowed to change it. Test `if (!f)` and only then use errno (through perror). The library never sets errno back to zero for you.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
question: `parse_port("80x")` runs `let n: u16 = s.trim().parse()?;` and the parse fails. What happens next?
options: `parse_port` returns `Err(...)` to its caller immediately, and `Ok(n)` is never reached
`n` is set to 0 and the function continues
The program panics with an InvalidDigit message
`?` skips the bad character and parses "80"
explain: `?` on an `Err` returns that error from the enclosing function at once, like `return Err(e)`. The caller decides what to do; in the example it prints the debug form of the error. Panicking is what `unwrap()` would do instead.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
question: A builder type has `fn finish(self) -> Report`, and you call `let r = builder.finish();`. What can you do with `builder` afterwards?
options: Nothing: it was moved into `finish`, so any later use is E0382
Read its fields, since only its methods are consumed
Call `finish` again, because methods can always be called repeatedly
Use it until the end of the scope, where it is dropped
explain: A `self` receiver takes ownership, exactly like passing the value to a function by value. `builder` is moved-from after the call, and the method decided what happened to its contents (here, turning them into a `Report`).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
question: Why is `thread::spawn(|| println!("{v:?}"))` rejected when `v` is a local Vec, while calling the same closure directly in `main` works?
options: Closures cannot capture a Vec
`println!` is not thread safe
Vec cannot be used from more than one thread
